title: SIFT — Scale-Invariant Feature Transform
summary: Local features invariant to scale and rotation, with distinctive descriptors that can be matched across very different photographs.
context: Lowe introduced SIFT for object recognition (ICCV 1999) and published the full method in IJCV (2004), one of the most cited papers in computer science.
contribution: Made wide-baseline matching between unordered, uncalibrated photographs reliable — the missing piece for fully automatic Structure from Motion.
technicalExplanation: Keypoints are extrema of a difference-of-Gaussians scale space; each receives a canonical orientation and a 128-D descriptor of gradient-orientation histograms. Matches are found by nearest-neighbour search with a ratio test.
historicalSignificance: Ended the dependence on small baselines and on manual tie points. Photo Tourism, Building Rome in a Day, VisualSFM and COLMAP all rely on SIFT or its descendants.
limitations: Patented until 2020; computationally expensive; struggles with strong illumination change and repetitive texture.

title: Splatting and EWA surface splatting
summary: Rendering volumes and point sets by projecting ('splatting') reconstruction kernels onto the image, with Gaussian kernels for anti-aliasing.
context: Westover introduced splatting for volume rendering (1990). Zwicker et al. (2001) formulated elliptical weighted average (EWA) splatting of Gaussian kernels for high-quality point-based surface rendering.
contribution: Derived how a 3D Gaussian kernel projects to a 2D Gaussian under a locally affine camera approximation — the exact projection used by 3D Gaussian Splatting.
technicalExplanation: A 3D Gaussian with covariance Σ projects to an image-space Gaussian with covariance Σ′ = J W Σ Wᵀ Jᵀ (W view transform, J Jacobian of projection). Splats are blended in depth order.
historicalSignificance: A graphics lineage that, two decades later, became central to reconstruction when Kerbl et al. made splatting differentiable and optimised the Gaussians from photographs.
limitations: Points were inputs from scanners, not optimised; no view-dependent appearance learning.

title: Semi-Global Matching
summary: Dense stereo by aggregating matching costs along multiple 1D paths — accurate, efficient and robust.
context: Published at CVPR 2005 and in TPAMI 2008, SGM was quickly adopted in aerial photogrammetry (dense DSMs from digital aerial imagery), automotive stereo and satellite mapping.
contribution: Brought near-global-optimisation quality to pixel-wise dense matching at practical cost.
technicalExplanation: A cost volume C(p, d) (e.g. mutual information or Census) is smoothed by dynamic programming along 8–16 directions with penalties P1 (small disparity changes) and P2 (discontinuities); disparities are chosen by winner-takes-all on the summed costs.
historicalSignificance: Arguably the most influential dense matcher in production photogrammetry; it turned digital aerial blocks into dense surface models and true orthophotos.
limitations: Streaking artefacts; struggles with textureless and reflective surfaces.

dates.adoption: Aerial DSM production c. 2008–; automotive stereo

title: Photo Tourism and Bundler
summary: Fully automatic Structure from Motion on unordered internet photo collections, with an interface to browse photos in 3D.
context: Presented at SIGGRAPH 2006 and commercialised as Microsoft Photosynth; the open-source Bundler implementation (2008) spread incremental SfM throughout research.
contribution: Combined SIFT matching, robust two-view geometry, incremental camera registration and repeated bundle adjustment into a robust pipeline for uncontrolled imagery.
technicalExplanation: Pairwise SIFT matching → RANSAC-verified fundamental matrices → track building → initial pair reconstruction → incremental resection (DLT/P3P) and triangulation → bundle adjustment after each addition. Focal lengths are initialised from EXIF.
historicalSignificance: Demonstrated that the camera network need not be designed: geometry can be recovered from whatever images exist.
limitations: Quadratic matching cost; drift; no metric scale without control.

dates.improvements: Building Rome in a Day (2009); VisualSFM (2011); COLMAP (2016)

title: Poisson surface reconstruction
summary: Watertight meshes from oriented point clouds by solving a Poisson equation for an indicator function.
context: Published at the Symposium on Geometry Processing 2006; the screened variant (2013) became the default meshing step for MVS point clouds.
contribution: A robust global method to turn noisy, dense point clouds into surfaces.
technicalExplanation: Find indicator χ whose gradient best matches the oriented normal field V: Δχ = ∇·V, solved on an adaptive octree; the surface is an iso-level of χ.
historicalSignificance: Completed the classical image → points → mesh pipeline used in heritage, VFX and surveying.
limitations: Requires consistent normals; tends to close holes (over-smoothing) in sparse regions.

title: Multi-View Stereo and PMVS
summary: Dense reconstruction from many calibrated images, benchmarked systematically and made practical by patch-based expansion.
context: Seitz et al. (2006) introduced the Middlebury multi-view stereo benchmark and taxonomy. Furukawa and Ponce's PMVS (CVPR 2007; TPAMI 2010) led the benchmarks and, with CMVS, scaled to SfM outputs.
contribution: Dense oriented patches grown from sparse seeds, filtered by visibility constraints — the standard dense step after Bundler/VisualSFM.
technicalExplanation: Patches (centre, normal) are optimised to maximise photometric consistency across visible images, expanded to neighbouring cells and filtered for visibility conflicts.
historicalSignificance: Together with SfM, completed fully automatic image-to-dense-model reconstruction available to anyone with a camera.
limitations: Output is points, not surfaces; struggles on textureless and specular regions.

dates.improvements: Depth-map fusion MVS; COLMAP MVS (2016); learned MVS (2018)

title: Visual SLAM
summary: Simultaneous localisation and mapping from a camera in real time.
context: MonoSLAM (Davison, 2003; TPAMI 2007) used filtering; PTAM (Klein & Murray, 2007) split tracking and keyframe bundle adjustment into parallel threads; ORB-SLAM (2015) added loop closure and relocalisation with binary features.
contribution: Turned SfM into an online, incremental process with real-time pose output — the basis of AR, robotics and spatial computing.
technicalExplanation: Tracking estimates the current pose by PnP against the map; mapping triangulates new points from keyframes and runs local bundle adjustment; loop closure detects revisits and corrects drift via pose-graph optimisation.
historicalSignificance: Shows photogrammetric estimation adapted to a temporal, causal stream — a precondition for real-time spatial reconstruction and Gaussian SLAM.
limitations: Sparse maps; scale drift in monocular systems; dynamic scenes violate assumptions.

dates.improvements: Direct methods (DTAM, LSD-SLAM), visual–inertial SLAM, Gaussian SLAM (2024)

title: Building Rome in a Day
summary: City-scale SfM from hundreds of thousands of internet photographs on a computing cluster.
context: Presented at ICCV 2009; showed reconstruction of Rome, Venice and Dubrovnik from Flickr photos within about a day.
contribution: Distributed matching (vocabulary trees, query expansion), skeletal graphs and parallel bundle adjustment for internet scale.
technicalExplanation: Image retrieval proposes candidate pairs; verified matches form a match graph; connected components are reconstructed independently with skeletal-set selection to reduce bundle adjustment size.
historicalSignificance: Scale became a research axis; it also showed the limits of incremental SfM, motivating global SfM methods.
limitations: Heavy computation; fragmented models; no georeferencing.

title: VisualSFM
summary: A GPU-accelerated, graphical SfM application that put automatic reconstruction in the hands of non-specialists.
context: Released around 2011 with SiftGPU and multicore bundle adjustment; the 2013 paper described near-linear-time incremental SfM. Combined with CMVS/PMVS it became a widely used free pipeline.
contribution: Speed and accessibility: preemptive matching, GPU features and efficient incremental BA.
technicalExplanation: Preemptive matching tests a subset of top-scale features before full matching; bundle adjustment runs on the full model only after geometric growth thresholds, keeping cost near-linear.
historicalSignificance: Widely used in archaeology, geoscience and education at the moment SfM entered surveying practice.
limitations: Closed source; limited maintenance after the mid-2010s.

title: SfM–MVS enters surveying practice
summary: Computer-vision reconstruction pipelines, consumer cameras and small UAVs were adopted in geoscience, heritage and surveying.
context: Commercial packages (e.g. Agisoft PhotoScan, Pix4D) and open-source tools (MicMac, VisualSFM) combined SfM, MVS and photogrammetric georeferencing. Westoby et al. (2012) helped popularise 'SfM photogrammetry' in geomorphology; consumer UAVs made aerial capture inexpensive.
contribution: Convergence: automated vision front-ends plus photogrammetric back-ends (ground control, self-calibration, accuracy assessment).
technicalExplanation: Uncalibrated or consumer cameras; automatic matching and self-calibrating bundle adjustment; georeferencing with GCPs or RTK; dense matching to DSMs, orthomosaics and textured meshes.
historicalSignificance: The moment the two lineages became indistinguishable in everyday practice, and when debates about rigour (systematic errors, 'doming', check-point accuracy) re-entered the vision-derived workflow.
limitations: Black-box software can hide systematic errors; accuracy reporting was often inconsistent.
uncertainty: The term 'SfM photogrammetry' is contested; photogrammetrists note the workflow is photogrammetry with automated orientation.

title: KinectFusion
summary: Real-time dense surface reconstruction with a consumer depth camera.
context: The Microsoft Kinect (2010) brought structured-light depth sensing to consumers; KinectFusion (ISMAR 2011) fused its depth stream on a GPU.
contribution: Interactive, dense, metric 3D capture by tracking against and fusing into a volumetric model.
technicalExplanation: Each depth frame is aligned to a raycast of the current model with ICP; then integrated into a truncated signed distance function (TSDF) on a GPU voxel grid.
historicalSignificance: Showed that sensing hardware (active depth) and GPUs could make reconstruction real-time; precursor of mobile LiDAR scanning apps.

title: Learned depth estimation and learned MVS
summary: Convolutional networks learned to predict depth from single images and to compute dense matching costs.
context: Eigen et al. (2014) predicted depth from a single image; MC-CNN (2015) learned stereo matching costs; MVSNet (2018) built differentiable plane-sweep cost volumes; MiDaS (2020) trained robust relative depth on mixed datasets.
contribution: Introduced learned priors into geometric estimation — geometry inferred partly from data statistics rather than only from parallax.
technicalExplanation: MVSNet warps deep features from source views onto fronto-parallel planes of the reference camera (homographies), builds a variance-based cost volume and regularises it with 3D CNNs to regress depth.
historicalSignificance: The first step toward feed-forward geometry; monocular depth priors are now used to regularise NeRF, 3DGS and dynamic reconstruction.
limitations: Scale ambiguity (monocular); dataset bias; weak uncertainty estimates.

title: COLMAP
summary: An open-source, general-purpose SfM and MVS pipeline that became the de facto standard for research.
context: Described in 'Structure-from-Motion Revisited' (CVPR 2016) and 'Pixelwise View Selection for Unstructured Multi-View Stereo' (ECCV 2016).
contribution: Robust geometric verification, next-best-view selection, robust triangulation and iterative BA/re-triangulation; probabilistic PatchMatch MVS with pixel-wise view selection.
technicalExplanation: Incremental SfM with scene-graph augmentation and verification; MVS estimates depth and normal per pixel jointly with view selection, then fuses depth maps into a point cloud and meshes with Poisson or Delaunay.
historicalSignificance: COLMAP poses are the starting point of almost all NeRF and 3DGS research; neural rendering thus inherits the photogrammetric camera model and its errors.
limitations: Slow on large collections; fails on textureless or very sparse captures — the gap feed-forward methods target.

dates.improvements: GLOMAP global SfM (2024); integration with learned features

title: Learned feature detection and matching
summary: Neural networks replaced handcrafted detectors, descriptors and matching heuristics.
context: SuperPoint (2018) learned keypoints and descriptors self-supervised; SuperGlue (2020) matched them with attention; LoFTR (2021) matched densely without detectors using transformers.
contribution: Robust correspondences under strong viewpoint and illumination change; attention-based reasoning over sets of features.
technicalExplanation: SuperGlue treats matching as an optimal transport problem over features refined by self- and cross-attention graph neural networks.
historicalSignificance: Attention across images is the conceptual step from learned matching to multi-view transformers that predict geometry directly (DUSt3R, VGGT).

title: Neural scene representations
summary: Scenes and shapes encoded as functions learned by neural networks, rendered differentiably.
context: In 2019 several works converged: DeepSDF and Occupancy Networks (implicit shape functions), Scene Representation Networks (SRN), and Neural Volumes (differentiable volume rendering of a learned voxel grid from multi-view video).
contribution: Established coordinate-based networks and differentiable rendering as a way to learn 3D from 2D supervision.
technicalExplanation: An MLP fθ maps a 3D coordinate (and possibly a latent code) to occupancy, signed distance or radiance; a differentiable renderer compares predicted and observed images, and gradients update θ.
historicalSignificance: The immediate antecedents of NeRF; they moved the 'representation' question to the centre of reconstruction research.
limitations: Low resolution or limited to objects; slow optimisation.
